name: Budgeting Fundamentals
description: Learn how to create and maintain a personal budget using the 50/15/5 rule. Build skills to track spending, set priorities, and avoid being broke.

final_exam_questions.question: What does the 50/15/5 budgeting rule recommend?
options: No more than 50% on essentials, 15% on retirement, 5% on emergency savings
final_exam_questions.explanation: The 50/15/5 rule: no more than 50% of take-home pay for essentials, 15% of pre-tax income for retirement, and 5% of take-home for emergency savings.

final_exam_questions.question: Why is it important to review your paycheck carefully?
options: To understand your gross pay, taxes, deductions, and net pay
final_exam_questions.explanation: Your paycheck shows gross pay, tax withholdings (FICA, federal, state), benefits deductions, and 401(k) contributions — all of which directly affect your take-home pay.

final_exam_questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a personal budget?
options: To know where your money goes so you can make informed choices
final_exam_questions.explanation: A budget helps you understand where your money goes, plan for financial goals, and avoid running out of money unexpectedly.

final_exam_questions.question: A budget is best described as:
options: A living document updated when circumstances change
final_exam_questions.explanation: A budget is a living document. It should be updated whenever your circumstances change — new job, new family member, buying a car, etc.

final_exam_questions.question: FICA taxes on your paycheck fund:
final_exam_questions.explanation: FICA (Federal Insurance Contributions Act) taxes fund Social Security and Medicare — both visible as separate line items on your pay stub.

name: Banking in the Modern World
description: Understand traditional banks, online banks, credit unions, debit cards, and payment services. Know how to choose the right bank and avoid costly fees.

final_exam_questions.question: What is FDIC insurance?
options: Federal protection for bank deposits up to $250,000 per account
final_exam_questions.explanation: FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per account — protecting you if a bank fails.

final_exam_questions.question: How does a debit card differ from a credit card?
options: Debit cards earn rewards; credit cards don't
Debit cards spend money directly from your checking account; credit cards borrow money
Credit cards require a PIN; debit cards don't
final_exam_questions.explanation: A debit card pulls money directly from your checking account. A credit card lets you borrow money from the bank to pay back later.

final_exam_questions.question: Why might an online bank offer better interest rates than a traditional bank?
options: They have no physical branches, so lower overhead costs
final_exam_questions.explanation: Online banks have lower operating costs (no physical branches) and pass those savings on as higher interest rates and lower fees.

final_exam_questions.question: What happens if you write a check for more than your checking account balance?
options: The bank covers the difference for free
You may face overdraft fees and the check may bounce
final_exam_questions.explanation: Writing a check without sufficient funds can result in overdraft fees, returned check fees, and damage to your financial reputation.

final_exam_questions.question: Credit unions differ from traditional banks in that they are:
options: Non-profit and member-supported, often offering lower rates
final_exam_questions.explanation: Credit unions are non-profit financial institutions owned by their members. They often offer lower interest rates on loans and higher rates on savings.

name: Credit, Debt & Smart Borrowing
description: Master credit scores, credit cards, Buy Now Pay Later, and debt repayment strategies. Learn to borrow smart and avoid the debt trap.

final_exam_questions.question: What order should you generally pay off debts?
options: Highest interest debts first (credit cards, then private loans, then car loans, then government loans, then mortgage)
Smallest balance first regardless of interest
final_exam_questions.explanation: Pay highest-interest debt first: credit cards, private student loans, car loans, then government student loans, and pay your mortgage last.

final_exam_questions.question: Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) is best used for:
options: Impulse buys and everyday food delivery
Planned, necessary larger purchases you can afford to repay on schedule
final_exam_questions.explanation: BNPL is most responsibly used for necessary, planned purchases (like a laptop or tires) where you've budgeted to repay on schedule.

final_exam_questions.question: What is the recommended credit card payment strategy?
options: Pay only the minimum each month
Pay the full balance every month to avoid interest
final_exam_questions.explanation: Paying your full credit card balance every month avoids interest charges, builds your credit history, and keeps your credit score healthy.

final_exam_questions.question: Which of these is 'good debt'?
options: Student loans or a home mortgage (assets that build future value)
Buy Now Pay Later for a coffee maker
final_exam_questions.explanation: Good debt is used to acquire assets that grow in value or increase earning potential — like education (student loans) or a home (mortgage).

final_exam_questions.question: A high credit score helps you by:
options: Allowing you to borrow money at lower interest rates
Eliminating the need to repay loans
final_exam_questions.explanation: A strong credit score signals creditworthiness to lenders, qualifying you for lower interest rates on mortgages, car loans, and other borrowing.

name: Investing Fundamentals
description: From stocks and bonds to ETFs and mutual funds — learn how to build a diversified investment portfolio and understand risk vs. reward.

final_exam_questions.question: What is a stock?
final_exam_questions.explanation: A stock (equity) represents fractional ownership in a corporation, entitling you to a share of its assets and profits.

final_exam_questions.question: Why is diversification important in investing?
options: It reduces risk by spreading investments across different assets
It focuses your money on the best one stock
It eliminates the need to research
final_exam_questions.explanation: Diversification reduces risk by spreading investments across different asset types, industries, and geographies — not all investments move together.

final_exam_questions.question: Which investment type is passively managed and typically tracks a market index?
final_exam_questions.explanation: ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds) are typically passively managed to track an index like the S&P 500, resulting in lower fees than actively managed funds.

final_exam_questions.question: The core principle of 'time in the market vs. timing the market' means:
options: Trade every day for best results
Staying invested long-term beats trying to predict market movements
Sell before a downturn every time
final_exam_questions.explanation: No one can consistently predict market timing. Staying invested long-term — through ups and downs — outperforms most active trading strategies.

final_exam_questions.question: What percentage of a young investor's portfolio should be in cryptocurrency, according to most financial advisors?
final_exam_questions.explanation: Most advisors recommend no more than 1–5% of your portfolio in crypto. The remaining 95%+ should be in diversified index funds or ETFs.

name: Saving & Building Wealth
description: Discover the power of compound interest, emergency funds, retirement accounts (401k, IRA, HSA), and strategies to build lasting financial security.

final_exam_questions.question: What is an emergency fund?
options: 3–6 months of living expenses saved for unexpected events
final_exam_questions.explanation: An emergency fund is 3–6 months of living expenses saved in an accessible account, protecting you from financial shock during job loss or unexpected expenses.

final_exam_questions.question: What is the benefit of contributing to a 401(k) up to your employer match?
options: You can withdraw it tax-free anytime
Your employer adds free money matching your contributions
final_exam_questions.explanation: An employer match is essentially free money added to your retirement savings. Not contributing enough to get the full match is leaving free money on the table.

final_exam_questions.question: A Health Savings Account (HSA) is special because:
options: It can only be used for gym memberships
Contributions, growth, and qualified withdrawals are all tax-free
Anyone can open one without a health plan
final_exam_questions.explanation: HSAs offer a triple tax advantage: contributions are pre-tax, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free.

final_exam_questions.question: The financial philosophy 'Save early, enough, and often' recommends saving what percentage of your income?
final_exam_questions.explanation: Saving 15–20% of your income is the recommended baseline to build wealth, fund retirement, and handle financial emergencies.

final_exam_questions.question: Compound interest is most powerful when you:
options: Start saving early and leave money invested for many years
final_exam_questions.explanation: Compound interest earns returns on your returns. The earlier you start and the longer you stay invested, the more dramatic the growth becomes.

name: AI Literacy: Using AI Responsibly and Effectively
description: A comprehensive 2-week program teaching you to understand, use, and critically evaluate AI. Learn practical skills, ethics, and responsible AI use through interactive activities.

final_exam_questions.question: Most AI systems used today are best described as:
final_exam_questions.explanation: Today's AI systems are narrow AI — excellent at specific tasks but not conscious or generally intelligent.

final_exam_questions.question: A model output that is fluent but factually wrong is often called:
final_exam_questions.explanation: Hallucination is when AI generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information.
